div.head: Many safety critical real-time systems, employ fault tolerant strategies in order to provide predictable pelformance in the presence of failures. One technique commonly employed is time redundancy using retry/ re-execution of tasks. This can in tum affect the correctness of the system by causing deadlines to be missed. This paper provides exact schedulability tests for fault tolerant task sets under specijed failure hypothesis,
Introduction
div.p: Real-time systems with high dependability requirements are traditionally built with massive replication and redundancy. The main objective is to maintain the properties of correctness and timeliness even in the event of faults. In certain classes of application, due to space, weight and cost considerations it may not be feasible to provide space redundancy. Such systems need to exploit time redundancy techniques. Due to the real-time nature of these systems, it is essential that the exploitation of time redundancy for correctness does not jeopardize the timeliness attribute. This underlines the need for feasibility analysis which provides guarantees for fault-tolerant real-time task sets under the assumption of a defined failure hypothesis. This paper provides such analysis.

Research into fixed priority scheduling theory has mainly focussed on the provision of feasibility tests which determine if a given task set is schedulable [7] [lo] [51. Such tests have been developed for increasingly less restrictive computational models, thus allowing tasks to interact via shared resources, to have deadlines less than their periods [ 11, release jitter [ 11, deadlines greater than their periods [13]. Finally, schedulability analysis has been extended to take account of the operating system kernel overheads found in real systems

div.head: U].
div.p: There are few papers which specifically deal with timing and scheduling issues in fault-tolerant systems. Ban-nister and Trivedi have studied the task allocation problem for fault-tolerant systems like SIFT [2]. They did not however consider schedulability or resource constraints.

Liestman and Campbell [6] proposed a set of scheduling algorithms for frame based, simply periodic uniprocessor systems. Thuel [ 121 developed reservation algorithms for scheduling fault recovery modules and dynamic on-line redundant time allocation strategies based on the concept of slack stealing.

Finally, Pandya and Malek [8] analysed the schedulability of a set of periodic tasks that are scheduled using rate monotonic priority assignment and are susceptible to a single fault. Their suggested model of recovery is reexecution of all unfinished tasks, while maintaining task priorities. They provide a bound of 0.50 for the minimum achievable utilization which compares favourably with the value of 0.69/2=0.345 (which follows from Liu and Layland's analysis [7]).

Performing schedulability analysis under fault assumptions could result in increased robustness and designer confidence. There is a tendency to relax the timing constraints upon occurrence of a fault. But we feel that guaranteeing a minimum level of performance in case of faults is extremely important in systems which are safety or mission critical. This can only be achieved by strictly adhering to the hard deadlines of critical tasks.

In this paper, we provide an exact feasibility test for faulttolerant task sets under specified failure hypothesis. Here we are able to provide guarantees for task sets with much higher utilizations than provided by [8].

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. In the next section, we outline a computational model and also describe a procedure for the feasibility testing of task sets without fault tolerance. Section 3 builds upon this model of task behaviour by adding a fault model. Feasibility analysis is given in section 4 for software fault tolerant techniques such as task re-execution, forward error recovery and recovery blocks. Given a fault hypothesis, the WCET of each task can be calculated using such analysis, this is illustrated using a simple example. Section 5 deals with the feasibility analysis if we resort to checkpointing schemes to take care of hardware faults. Finally section 6 offers our conclusions.

div.head: Computation Model
div.p: In this paper we consider only a uniprocessor system, the results are however equally applicable to distributedmultiprocessor systems, where task allocation to individual processors is performed statically. The computational model assumed does not impose any restrictions on the priority assignment algorithm used. This could be Rate Monotonic, Deadline Monotonic or any other priority assignment algorithm. We assume that each task is assigned a unique priority and that a task can be immediately preempted by a higher priority task. At run time, the highest priority task from the set of runnable tasks is allocated processor time.

We assume a set of n tasks, (TI, ~2 , . . T,) in which tasks are ordered according to the assigned priorities, where 1 denotes the highest priority and n denotes the lowest priority. Each task T, is assumed to have a minimum inter-arrival time T,, worst case execution time (WCET) C, and deadline D,.

Each task T, may be blocked by lower priority tasks for at most B, units of time as a result of the operation of the Priority Ceiling Protocol [ 111. div.head: Fault model and assumptions
div.p: We are primarily concerned with providing scheduling guarantees in fault-tolerant systems which employ time redundancy. Here the basic assumption is that a large variety of transient and intermittent hardware and software faults can be effectively overcome by simple re-execution of the affected task or by executing an alternate action.

We assume that a fault can adversely affect only one task at a time and is detected at the end of that task's execution. Although somewhat pessimistic, this assumption is realistic since in many implementations, task errors are detected by acceptance tests or watchdog timerdfences which are executed at the end of task execution. In case of tasks communicating via shared resources, we assume that an acceptance test is executed before passing an output value to another task. This is essential to avoid the domino effect [9] due to fault propagation.

For the system to tolerate faults, the inter-arrival time between faults needs to be greater than a minimum value. For example, if the inter-anival time between faults is less than the computation time of any task, then the task set will not be schedulable in the presence of faults.

div.head: Forward error recovery
div.p: Forward error recovery schemes like exception handlers aim to nullify the effects of faulty execution and do some reinitialization, rather than performing the whole computation once again. In these situations, the amount of computation time required by the error handler 6% will be considerably 3, gives the response times of our example task set using forward recovery for fault handling. The column headed 'Exception handler' gives the execution time of exception handlers for each task. Here we show that the example task set which was not schedulable under our simple model with the minimum inter-arrival time of faults, TF = 200 is now schedulable under the forward error recovery model. It should however be noted that the quality of service provided by exception handlers is typically considerably lower than that obtained by re-execution of the task.

div.head: Recovery Blocks
div.p: The recovery block [4] was proposed as a method for program structuring and backward error recovery by combining design diversity with error checking and state restoration. Each recovery block consists of a primary module, one or more alternate modules and an acceptance test. A primary module is the preferred implementation of the algorithm for the task. An alternate is a diverse implementation of the same specification using a different algorithm.

Here the major difference from previous two models is that, the computation time required for the alternative could be greater than the computation time of the primary since in real-time systems the preferred algorithm tends to be the one with lower execution time. div.head: Utilization Bounds
div.p: Liu and Layland proved in [7] that a task set consisting of n independent periodic tasks is guaranteed to have a feasible schedule on a uniprocessor under rate monotonic priority assignment, as long as the utilization of the task set is less than n(2l/" -1). This bound approaches 0.693 as n tends to infinity. If we want to include fault tolerance capability into their analysis, the easiest way is to double the task execution times. This implies that a periodic task set scheduled using rate monotonic priority assignment and susceptible to a single fault is guaranteed to have a feasible schedule as long as the utilization of the task set is less than (2l/" -1), which tends to 0.346.

In [8], Pandya and Malek provided an improved bound for worst case achievable utilization. Their model of recovery is re-execution of all unfinished tasks, while maintaining task priorities. They provide a bound of 0.50 for the minimum achievable utilization which will guarantee the schedulability of the task set. The analysis reported above improves this bound by providing exact schedulability tests under specified failure hypothesis.

For example, consider the task set ( ~1 , 7 2 , 7 -3 , ~4 ) with C, = 1 , T, = 5, D, = 5 and B, = 0 for i=1,2,3,4. This task set has a utilization of 80% and hence we cannot guarantee the schedulability of this task set via Pandya and Malek's method. However, using the feasibility analysis derived in the previous section, it can be seen that the above task set is schedulable, under a single transient fault, provided the inter-arrival time between faults is greater than 5.

One major difference between our fault model and Pandya and Malek's approach should be noted, since it is the main contributing factor in the improvement in the minimum utilization bound in our case. Pandya and Malek's analysis assumes that recovery is achieved by re-execution of all unfinished tasks. We assume that upon fault occurrence, it is only necessary to re-execute the current task. This assumption is justifiable since we insist that an acceptance test be executed before passing data to other tasks.

div.head: Checkpoints
div.p: Checkpoint schemes were originally proposed for improving the reliability of database systems and similar transaction oriented systems. Checkpointing in a real-time system has some important differences compared to that employed in a database system. Normally a real-time task does not require an audit trail, since all the data is assumed to be local upon initiation of the task. The saved state of the task, which consists of values of data variables and contents of system registers, is called a checkpoint. To ensure correctness of a checkpoint, an acceptance test must be executed before saving the necessary data [9]. Tasks are allowed to exchange data via shared memory, but again an acceptance test needs to be executed before passing data to other tasks.

From Tables 2 and3 it can be seen that the schedulability of a task set under faults, can be improved if we can reduce the additional computation time requirement after fault occurrence. This explains the improved schedulability under the exception handler scheme. However, in case of exception handlers, after a fault the service quality is normally lower. Checkpointing the tasks which have the maximum response times is another way of reducing the computation requirements after fault occurrences without causing any deterioration in the service quality. The task set is the same one used in Tables 1 and2, which was not previously schedulable under a fault inter-arrival time of 200 units. It can be seen that by checkpointing the response times have reduced considerably and the task set is now schedulable.

Note that WCET values now include the checkpoint overhead. Further, the checkpoint interval shown is the largest value. If there was no overhead involved in checkpointing, then we might as well checkpoint after every instruction. However, since there is an overhead, checkpointing will be beneficial only for tasks with computation time greater than checkpoint overhead. Also a lower bound for the checkpoint interval is the checkpoint overhead. Adding further checkpoints increases the response time beyond that found for our simple model for re-executing the task.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper, we presented an exact feasibility test for task sets scheduled using any fixed priority preemptive scheme and which can tolerate a certain class of faults. Compared to other known schemes, our schedulability equations can guarantee task sets with higher utilization bounds. We aim to extend these notions to encompass other classes of failures in future as well as to suggest optimal checkpoint strategies.
